doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: His early sound and how he teaches embouchure
summary: His clamped peashooter sound, Noah Brandmark's sound, and how he teaches students to find a full sound.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Did you actually play with your upper lip under your teeth?

Well he had, put your head down a little bit, you know he taught Stan Getz and all his students. But I don’t think you need this other than support and with the slightest support, just be centered in the middle of the mouthpiece. But I have a friend, Noah Brandmark that played with Woody Herman, that had a great sound. And it took me until I was about 30 to have a sound like him, and he was 14 when we met. He was only studying a half year with Bill Shiner and he had this mature sound. I wasn’t jealous we were just close friends. But he’d play over here. We’d be silly. He’d play anywhere and get a great sound. And I could do that now too. If you have the pressure from the reed, you know, what makes the reed vibrate? It’s just this — if you had a piece of wood and air going

through it you don’t need your lip. I’m being silly. Or cardboard. And make it vibrate. I was just clamping on the opening of the reed. So I have them start from nothing and blow, and blow as full as you can, but when your lip is on the reed if you’re not putting any pressure at all it’s not going to vibrate yet. So I said slowly get tighter and eventually clamp the reed. And back off slowly until you are vibrating. And you’re getting like, I call it a buzz like in your oral cavity. I can’t explain it. But it’s ahh, like an opera singer, where you’re getting the fullest sound and you’re not doing anything, you have enough air to support it, like a good faucet that works, if you want full volume you can play loud, but you should get that buzz on a soft note too, like [scats] you know? Whatever. And they find the center and all of a sudden for the first time in their life they get the sound and they sound like me for a minute. Like on a G, like a good note, not too low, not too high because C is a little funny. A G — I says, “You got it.” I said I don’t have to say anything more. Now you know.
